Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Are the Spanish really anti-tourists? It seems they want to bite the hand that feeds them.
Answer: I spent two months in the Iberian Peninsula last year. My feeling is actually that Lisbon had the most complaints about Airbnb’s and tourism. I went to a bar and the bartender read me the riot act about how we Americans were ruining the city, raising the rent, ruining the local culture, and that we could fuck off. No one got that upset with me in Spain. Overall, I still like Portugal better though. That was one of the only negative interactions I had. Hahaha. (Lisbon. This neighborhood has been completely overtaken by Airbnb’s. The locals HATE this. My experience in Spain was much more generally cold though, but no one ever specifically gave me problems like in Portugal. Photo by author.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What types of weapons can the American military mount onto its vehicles?
Answer: I can tell you the absolutely coolest weapon system I saw mounted on a humvee during the War in Iraq. A freakin’ minigun! (Special Operations personnel usually had their humvees set up something like this in Baghdad.) This thing can fire between 2,000 and 6,000 rounds per minute up to maximum range of about 1,000 meters. An absolute beast of a weapon to unleash on the ground. A runner up: Common Remotely Operated Weapon Station (CROWS). CROWS was brand new when I deployed to Iraq, so it’s probably old hat by now, but to us it was something out of the future. It allows a weapon to be fired from inside the protection of the vehicle, without exposing the gunner. Gunners were almost always the first to be injured or killed in battle or by roadside bombs, since they’re exposed. CROWS changed all of that. (Two soldiers with the CROWS system. Image credit: Wikipedia.) (Vehicles equipped with CROWS on convoy duty, Baghdad. Image credit: Wikipedia.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Why do some rich people claim to be "miserable" despite having better lives than literally 99% of the population?
Answer: Rich people can be just as miserable or in some cases, more miserable than your average person. Now, let’s not completely buy into the myth that money can’t buy happiness on some level. If you’re a subsistence farmer in Afghanistan and suddenly find your way into enough money to move to a western nation, to live in a comfortable home with a refrigerator stuffed with all of your favorite Afghani snacks and an iPhone with all of your favorite Afghani songs — you will almost certainly be happier than you were before. However, after all of your basic needs are met, the relationship between money and happiness is less clear. (Christina with her father, Aristotle. Photo credit: El Mundo newspaper.) Take for example, Christina Onassis. Christina was the only daughter of Greek shipping magnate Aristotle Onassis. Within a short period of time, Christina had both of her parents and her older brother die, leaving her with a fortune worth hundreds of millions of dollars at only age 24. So, by the time she inherited her personal fortune, she had already suffered through some incredibly difficult circumstances. Additionally, she went on to develop a prescription drug problem, suffered from constant issues with her weight, and bouts of depression. Furthermore, her love life was a complete mess and she married (and divorced) a total of four times all before the age of 37. By the time she was 37, the effects of her chaotic and miserable life had taken its toll on her and she died of a heart attack. Wealth can buy you a very nice chateau, yachts, and ski vacations in St. Moritz. What it can’t guarantee you is that you will lead a life free or misery, or that you will have good health, or even that you will live a long life.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: People who grew up poor then entered the middle class as adults, what changes did you notice the most?
Answer: I noticed that most aspects of life are easier, but not all of them. I have been middle class for nearly all of my adult life, but grew up in urban poverty in Detroit. I think that living in America’s middle class is a very fortunate place to be in society, especially when compared to life, globally. However, I think it’s interesting that America’s middle class comes across as the most worried and anxious in life, but maybe that’s because they make up most of the population. Or it could be my opinion because these are the people with which I am most familiar. When I was poor we had worries, but in some ways we worried less, because we had less to lose. Middle class Americans live very similar lives in that we are college educated or work in a trade, live in the suburban areas of large cities (with a few exceptions), often work Monday - Friday types of jobs, take yearly vacations, and own our own homes. The biggest problems faced by the middle class are: (1) the price of admission into a middle class life has risen steeply. Particularly, college and professional education. (2) For most middle class Americans, their health insurance is tied to their job or small business. Long term illness can be a very real threat to your way of life, should you encounter it. Those two things cover probably 70% of the worries of middle class Americans. Just two issues, but they’re both incredibly expensive issues. Living around other middle class people means hearing them complain about these issues all of the time. Keep in mind though, most middle class people are from middle class homes. To them, the world seems worse, because they don’t have the same lifestyle their parents had at a similar age. For those of us from poverty that are middle class, we have a much different outlook on what it means to be middle class. We are usually much more grateful.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Is the United States in decline?
Answer: A search of Google reveals that the Fast & Furious franchise has brought in a total revenue of $7 billion dollars since its initial release in 2001. Lesotho, a landlocked nation in Africa, home to over 2 million people, has an annual gross domestic product of about $2.2 billion dollars. Lesotho has the 184th strongest economy in the world. It is close to the bottom, but it’s actually not in last place. Lesotho’s entire economy could fit safely within the revenue of the Fast & Furious franchise, even if it tripled in size. Keep in mind, this is just a single media franchise. What’s even more interesting about the Fast & Furious film franchise is where it makes most of its money. That is, outside of the United States. More than $5 billion dollars of the $7 billion dollars in revenue was brought in from international ticket sales, of which the most important market is China. China, the country said to be America’s greatest geopolitical rival, is also the largest consumer of American pop culture. So, I don’t know, questioner. Is America in decline and if so, relative to who? (I suspect that once the US is in decline the global appetite for these dumb fucking movies about cars will be satiated. Until then, there is no hope. The cinema, dominated by American corporatism, is not a joyful place. Image source: IMDB).

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Who uses the euro?
Answer: A lot of countries. Interestingly enough, a few countries in the Americas use the Euro. When exchange rates were less favorable, this made vacations less enjoyable. These countries also tend to charge a rather high amount for currency conversion from the US dollar to the Euro. Some years ago I was in Saint Martin in the Caribbean and we went for a short day trip over to Saint Bart’s on a catamaran. It was a fun experience, but I remember stopping into some tourist shop and there was a man there with an obvious New York accent. He politely asked the shop attendant how much a T-shirt in the shop would cost. I think it was something like €25, but they wanted $35 if he was going to pay in dollars. He got incredibly upset. “This place is a third world country! You’re hardly suckin’ air. You would be NOTHING without America!” I was a bit embarrassed by my fellow American. But he was also right. The price was too god damned high for a simple t-shirt. (St. Bart’s. This island is a part of France, so they use the Euro. Don’t expect anything to be cheap in this playground for the rich and famous. Photo by author.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Which type of stolen valor is more prevalent, non-soldiers pretending they are soldiers, or soldiers pretending they’re more important or heroic than they are?
Answer: Yeah, so it’s much harder to fake being in the military if you have never served. I’m not saying it’s impossible. But it’s nearly impossible for someone who didn’t serve in the military to pass for military around military guys for very long. It will all come apart fairly quickly. For a time I worked in private security and one of the other employees lied about serving in the military. This was quickly discovered by me when he didn’t know what a DD-214 was. Seriously, the most basic of military shit. You can’t make it up. To anyone not familiar, the DD-214 is the document that releases us from government slavery. Every single Iraqi Freedom and Enduring Freedom veteran EVER knows what a DD-214 is. However, verifying individual events or even units is much more difficult and you can’t really call anyone out on anything with certainty (unless you see their service record). At the same company, a guy swore that he served in SWCC in the Navy (the elite unit tasked with transporting Navy SEALS by boat). To us, he seemed like a really out of shape idiot with his head constantly up his ass. We more or less tolerated his stories, but always with a healthy dose of suspicion. If he was lying, it was kind of an intelligent lie. He didn’t say Navy SEAL because that might have been too unbelievable amongst a lot of veterans (and we may have taken the initiative to contact someone). SWCC, on the other hand, is cool, but not so cool we ever called him on his bullshit and asked him to show us his record. (Everyone with recent service in the US military knows what a DD-214 (military discharge document) is. There are even a few companies that make DD-214 blankets so veterans can sleep sound knowing they never have to deal with the military again. Photo credit: Amazon.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What is an interesting fact of history that most people don't know?
Answer: Colombia’s participation in the Korean War. Just after the outset of the Korean War, conservative president Laureano Gómez, won election in Colombia. He sought closer ties with the United States, which was now fighting a war in Korea. The United States requested that several countries in the Americas send troops to aid in its efforts, including Mexico and Brazil. Only Colombia answered. (Soldiers of the Colombian Battalion with an American army officer. Photo source: Wikipedia). Colombia sent approximately 5,000 soldiers (Colombian Battalion - Wikipedia) and three frigates to Korea to assist United Nations actions in Korea in 1951, spearheaded by the United States. Given the relative smallness of the Colombian military, this contribution was significant. The Colombians fought honorably and with distinction, earning several awards from both the US and Korean governments including numerous Silver Stars and Bronze Stars for valor. (Colombian soldiers with the insignia of the Colombian Battalion on their ascots. Photo source: Wikipedia). Of particular note, the Battle of Old Baldy, was the single deadliest battle for the Colombian Battalion, which suffered 97 men killed in action. Approximately 20% of the unit’s fighting strength at the time. The Colombians returned home after the war ended in 1954. They suffered approximately 200 men killed in action and several hundred more wounded in action. (A statue paying tribute to Colombia in South Korea. Source: South Korea - Colombia - Korean War Memorials). Today, in most of the world, Colombia’s particpation in the war is all but forgotten. In Colombia, there are monuments and plaques in several cities displaying Colombia’s contribution to the war effort and acknowledging the sacrifices of their Korean War veterans. The other legacy of the war; South Korea quickly established diplomatic ties with Colombia. A few Koreans later immigrated to Colombia, particularly the capital. Today, there is a tiny, but very present Korean community in Bogota. Of course, there are several tasty Korean restaurants too.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Do you think technology is making us more disconnected from each other?
Answer: Yes, especially politically speaking. Online political rhetoric, in my opinion, is responsible for the highly charged political atmosphere we all live in today. It’s hazardous to become “friends” on Facebook or other social media with co-workers, friends, and even some family members. Some time ago, one of my friends told me that her niece blocked her uncle on Facebook because he wouldn’t stop posting pro-life material, something she feels very strongly against. Now they rarely speak in person anymore either. Just a couple of decades ago, no one had a platform to constantly badger others with their political beliefs. Politics was something people talked about much more rarely. Maybe just a few times a year. Everyone eventually had some laughs about it around the dinner table or the bar and went home more or less unscathed. That kind of polite discussion around politics really isn’t possible anymore.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Is it currently safe to travel to Peru with the state of emergency in place?
Answer: I have a friend, a fellow veteran, that sometimes travels with me to dangerous places. Last month he returned from several weeks in Peru, completely alone. He said it was interesting for the hiking, otherwise unremarkable and boring. His feelings largely mirror my own. If you travel to Peru right now you’ll almost certainly be safe. Avoid areas where protestors may gather. Stay alert to the changing threats by monitoring news and travel alerts. Register your location and phone number with your embassy. Most importantly, only drink bottled water. Other than that, you should be okay. (Riding ATV’s in the Peruvian countryside. Photo by author). I’m not sure if you are a US citizen or not, but the US embassy in Lima does a good job at posting alerts when there are planned protests or a change in the security situation. Currently, they are not advising against travel to Peru, and the US embassy tends to be the most paranoid.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Is it true that all Canadians are friendly? What about those living in Quebec?
Answer: I’m going to disagree with other people. Having lived and spent a considerable time in southern Mexico, I can tell you that the opinion of Canadians here, particularly French Canadians, is rather mixed. There is a large population of Quebecois who live here either full time or part time to escape the Canadian winters. (Our friendly neighborhood cat that lived at the bar. Photo by author.) Story time: during the COVID-19 pandemic, Mexico was subject to rather severe restrictions. To our endless annoyance, nearly all bars and restaurants were restricted to closing at 10 pm for all of 2021 and even part of 2022. One night I was at my local bar run by a friend of mine in Merida. It must have been 9:50 or something close to that. Just as my friend was ready to close the bar a group of French Canadians showed up to the bar. My friend regretfully informed the group that he could not serve them since the bar would be closing in just 10 minutes. In short order they expressed their outrage. My friend, ever polite, didn’t want to do anything to offend them. I sat merely observing the entire ordeal. Finally, one of the men took out a $500 peso note and slammed it on the bar “this is Mexico! You will open this fucking bar!” Unbeknownst to these idiots, the fine for staying open during COVID restrictions was at least $10,000 pesos. Not nearly enough money to break the law. At this point I said what my friend was thinking: “you don’t have enough money, so get the fuck out of here!” They did as I said. It felt good to do a little justice in the world. After living in Mexico I have always joked that Canada is a polite country because they make all the jerks leave. You can often find them in the Yucatán region of Mexico.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Do you think it is fair for the New York Times editorial board to call for President Biden to exit the presidential election contest based on his debate performance?
Answer: Yes. Look, presidential debates, to a large degree, are about showmanship. None of us give a shit about the talking points either candidate is going to discuss. We’ve already heard them all. A significant reason we hold these debates is because we want to get the presidential candidates out in front of us where we can see them and get a good look at how they perform under a bit of pressure. If the debate was a test of those skills, Biden failed horribly. Terrifyingly. Sure, president Biden may have had a cold or other factors affecting his performance. But he is currently the President! Given the current state of our world today, at any moment he could be called on to make important decisions that not only affect Americans, but all of humanity. That is the kind of burden our president carries at all times. After seeing how he performed in a simple debate last night, do we really want to leave the fate of humanity up to this man? I think not. We need to do better, much better as a nation. The mere fact that the election is between these two grumpy old men is a testament to that. (Photo credit: AL.com)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: If someone is fatally wounded, should you tell him?
Answer: I’m not a medic, so it’s actually not my job to tell someone if they’ll make it or not. I usually didn’t know for sure. In my military career I would say I encountered a few people who were obviously going to die, but I didn’t say anything. I think they already knew anyhow. You comfort the person as best as you can and wait for the medics. (Air Force tactical casualty care. Photo credit: US Air Force.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Why is downtown in US cities often considered unsafe after dark, when it's normally the safest areas in European cities?
Answer: I don’t know that this is true. Crime isn’t likely to happen to you in most downtown areas of the US. Crime happens mostly in residential areas. Downtowns tend to be business and entertainment centers where violent crime, in particular, is exceedingly rare. Let’s take a look at two violent American cities I know very well. My hometown of Detroit and adoptive hometown of Cleveland: I have outlined the downtowns in red. Darkly shaded areas have the most crimes reported. (Detroit, neighborhoodscout.com) (Cleveland, beighborhoodscout.com) Neither city’s downtown has high crime compared to neighborhoods where people live. However, if you look closely at both maps you can see how much crime can vary just from postal code to postal code in American cities. Both cities have neighborhoods that are directly adjacent to downtown that do have high crime. Both are home to low income housing projects. Visitors or the few people that live downtown in these cities aren’t likely to wander there.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What is the typical "military type" of person, or is there such a thing?
Answer: Instead of focusing on whether there is a military type, let me give you some perspective from inside. I have found that nearly all military units I have been with have people who possess similar traits. This is my perspective as an enlisted airman in the US Air Force. The people you meet in the military are as follows: Lifer: generally squared away, but is not the sharpest nor the dullest in the shed. He is in it for the long term. Lives and breathes the military, because that’s all he has. By year 15 of his career he is either solidly married or twice-divorced. A bit overweight. Swears when he needs to, doesn’t go overboard. Drinks hard only on the weekends these days. Jaded Senior NCO: an asshole. He hates you. He hates your ugly wife. He hates your family, especially the mother that created you. You cretin. He has only 2–3 years to retirement. Barely gets a word out without swearing and telling you that you and your entire squad are “fucked up like Chinese money.” Is definitely twice divorced. When he retires he will pick up a civilian government job closely related to what he used to do. Is actively an alcoholic. Drinks every day. Bible Thumper: the most boring guy in your unit. He has a large bible as well as a small bible with a camouflage cover. The small bible is always in one of his pockets. We only hang out with him if we need a designated driver from a bar or strip club. Doesn’t drink, doesn’t smoke, doesn’t swear. Doesn’t believe in pre-marital sex. Single and a virgin. See…like I said, boring. Womanizer: this is the guy who always has a new lady on his arm. Sometimes they are civilians, sometimes he poaches the base population. There are always whispers about him. “I heard he banged the supply sergeant with big tits!” “Bro, I heard it was the new squadron XO!” Always has a fresh haircut and sharp uniform. Fun to hang out with after duty. Swears constantly, especially when talking about his sexual escapades. Real hedonist. Binge drinker on the weekends, just beer on the weekdays. Occasionally, a line of coke. Teetotaler: is actually a cool guy, but he had to give up drinking because he was out of control when he was a young airman. He actually likes hanging out with the guys, he just won’t drink. He comes to work and does his job. Keeps a neat appearance, but the goal is to stay under the radar. Goes home to an Asian wife and kids who actually enjoy having him in their life. Only swears when telling stories about the good old days. Nerd: today you see a lot of this personality type in the military. These are the guys who joined up to pay for college. They can make the worst airmen, since they do tend to have a lot of book smarts. They question orders where others woud not. His uniform and appearance could use some work. Swears a lot, especially when talking about which Star Wars is the best Star Wars. Is single. Drinks daily, but drinks weird shit like Pabst Blue Ribbon. Jaded Black NCO: is from a place like Philadelphia, Baltimore, or some southern town you’ve never heard of. Swearing is a part of his personality. He hates the military and secretly and sometimes not-so-secretely hates white people. Motivation for military service is simple: he wants to get every buck out of Uncle Sam that he can. For lack of more stable options, he is also a lifer at this point. His uniform and haircut are always sharp. One of his auxillary duties is to pull aside all new black unit members and give the lay of the land. He has a wife, kids, and a couple of girlfriends. Drinks some weekends and on special ocassions. Attends church. The lieutenant has recently asked him to stop using so much profanity, especially when people from other squadrons can hear him. Alcoholic: in an organization that loves heavy drinking, those labeled alcoholics are the absolute heaviest of drinkers. They frequently are too ill to come to work, show up for duty drunk, or get caught driving under the influence on the weekends. If the person is a senior NCO or officer, they’ll almost always have someone to cover for them to protect their careers. For senior NCO’s, they’ll be put in a position where they can’t hurt anyone or break anything until their time is up in the military. Divorced. This person is profane, untrusthworthy, and usually disheveled in appearance. Patriots: this personality is the rarest of them all. These are people who join the military with their main reason being to serve and fight. They are often religious. They come from a long line of men who served. They are conservative, already well-versed the use of firearms and living off the land. Neat uniform and appearance. Rarely swears, drinks socially. Knows a lot of racist jokes. Spends his off duty time hunting, fishing, and driving a big fuckin’ truck. Has a pretty blonde girlfriend he is thinking about marrying. American dream. Future divorcee, Jaded NCO, and alcoholic. Commanding Officers: are so stereotypically the same, you can substitute one for another. All went to a four year university or a military academy. They always have an impeccable appearance and uniforms that are starched and creased in all of the right places. Usually fit. Their activities both on and off-duty mystify enlisted men. We don’t know what he does on duty besides sitting behind a desk with a computer with big stacks of paper. Off duty, he has weird hobbies like tennis, triathlons, and chess. In a stable marriage with kids. Only uses swear words sparingly, and then only “damn” or “hell.” Only has a couple of beers in front of the men to show his face. Is secretly having an affair with his clerk. (My squad doing land navigation training, Fort Bliss, El Paso, 2009. Photo by author.) Edit: this could all be based on memories, horribly offensive stereotypes, or both.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What the craziest situation you've encountered being in the military?
Answer: Let me paint you a picture. It’s sometime around midnight on Sather Air Base, Iraq. The year is 2009. There is a port-a-potty set up right next to our entry control point (ECP) to the air base. This ECP is right next to the end of the active runway, with only a chain link fence separating us from the runway. (C-17 Globemaster. Image credit: US Air Force.) Most of us are relaxing, playing cards and hoping that no one from command comes around and pesters us with stupid questions. One of our Ugandan security contractors gets up and goes to the port-a-potty. Just as he is doing so a huge C-17 cargo aircraft pulls to the end of the run way. The aircraft then turns 90 degrees, so that the rear of the aircraft is pointed directly at our ECP. While our unfortunate security contractor is inside taking a dump, the aircrew decide to do a run-up of all four of the aircraft’s powerful engines, directing the blast right at us. Sons of bitches! It kicked up a lot of rocks and debris, and made a metric fuck ton of noise. But most unfortunately, it manages to flip an entire port-a-potty with our 160lb Ugandan comrade inside! The port-a-potty is now lying flat on the ground with the door side facing up, thankfully. Hearing the muffled screams emanating from inside, we rush over to open the door to let our friend out. Unfortunately, a funny situation then arises, because as much as we want to help the man up, he’s now covered in blue water, urine, and shit. No one wanted to touch him. After some time someone had the courage to grasp his hand and lift him up. We sent him directly to medical for evaluation. He was okay, physically. I’m sure that no matter what else happened during his deployment, that was the most traumatic thing he experienced. (Port-a-potties at a deployed location, Baghdad. Photo by author.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Should we travel abroad or not?
Answer: I think this is a good question to ask in this day and age. There are some that will insist that we should all travel, that we should all get to know other countries, especially us Americans. However, the truth is that travel is not desired by everyone. It won’t suit everyone. It’s difficult to write a prescription for all of humanity. (Trying to find a boat to take me out on the bay, Puerto Escondido, Oaxaca. Photo by author.) There are also ethical concerns of travel like the effect of carbon emissions on climate change and gentrification. Of course, there are methods of travel that mitigate these problems, but are often impractical or much more expensive. I don’t see travel as essential for everyone that wants to be a well-rounded person. Besides, it’s not as if traveling is a panacea when it comes to ignorance about the world. Plenty of people go to all-inclusive resorts in Mexico, never leave the resort, and behave like assholes. This kind of person has been abroad, but it was hardly an educational or transformative experience. You can get what you need out of life where you are, or abroad. Which kind of person you are depends largely on which decision you should make. Are you curious, are you an explorer? Do you want to learn new languages, and eat foods you have never even heard of in your native country? Are you good at being alone? Traveling long term, as in more than a few weeks, almost always means traveling alone. (Lunch alone at OCI.mde in Medellin, Colombia. Photo by author.) Remember that travel is only one form of exploration. If you do decide to go abroad, be kind to the locals, it makes things easier for the next citizen of your country that comes after you.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Surveys: What was your college experience like?
Answer: Overall: awesome! I was the first of my family to go to college, so I didn’t really know what to expect. I received an academic scholarship, but would have to find a way to pay for room and board. It was expensive to attend a private Jesuit school, but the first two years of college especially, were incredibly fun. As a freshman, no one really expects too much out of you. You’ll have a lot on your plate between sports, social, and academic activities. For kids from working class or poor families like mine, we also had student jobs (almost all were insanely easy). (Detroit Mercy, where I spent the first two years of university before joining the military. Photo source: Association of Jesuit Colleges and Universities). My university was small by US standards. Only about 5,000 students. Practically all of us freshmen that lived on campus knew each other. We’d spent two weeks hiking, camping, and playing games during summer orientation. A few of us freshman had already established relationships with people over 21 on campus. This guaranteed we’d have a steady supply of alcohol. None of my male friends had a girlfriend nearby except for my friend, Chuy, who I actually knew from high school. I had promised my high school sweetheart that we’d keep going steady, but she was two hours away at Michigan State. On weekends I was either fencing, drinking heavily with my friends, visiting my girlfriend, or in rare cases, studying. Sometimes a combination of all of the above. (Épée fencing at Detroit Mercy. Source: University of Detroit Mercy). I remember very little about my studies other than to say it was fairly rigorous compared to life in Detroit public schools. Still, I didn’t take my studies serioiusly. I often skipped or showed up late to classes and had friends hand me their notes. I was the complete opposite of myself as a high school student. I knew that in the long term my grades wouldn’t really matter. Overall, I received slightly higher than average grades. Nothing special. I think that only my GMAT score allowed me to attend graduate school. Graduate school was different in that it was a much more serious environment. Missing an assignment just isn’t something that graduate students do. You’re also expected at every lecture unless you have a legitimately good excuse. Basically, your professors want you to behave like an adult. Some of your classmates are also much older than your average college student. When I graduated with my bachelor’s I was old for a college student. At 25 in graduate school, I was about average age, maybe slightly younger for once. Still, my friends and I would often show up to class after serious drinking sessions in a bar near campus. Weekends were still spent partying in and around Ann Arbor and Detroit with more funds (read: student loan or veterans’ benefits) than people in their 20’s should reasonably control. I think my college experience was about average for people my age that went to college in the 2000’s. We partied a lot, learned about life through relationships, studied as little as possible. Us guys fantasized about girls much more than we actually got to share our bed with them. Our activities outside of the classroom were sometimes foolish, dangerous, shameful, and reckless. As I said, about average.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: How do you define the American Dream?
Answer: My definition of the American dream is probably a bit interesting. When I was young, it meant growing up to live a life of adventure, financial stability, and a fair amount of violence. In that I succeeded, mostly. In the 1990’s we grew up on adventure and spy flicks. We always knew who the bad guys were, even if they didn’t always wear black hats. Americans were confident and self-assured and always the hero. (Three Kings. A movie of my childhood fantasies. Image credit: Amazon.) To me, achieving the American dream, ironically, meant leaving America. It meant going to interesting places, learning the local culture, and appreciating the food. Americans, by nature, are explorers (despite what you might hear here on Quora). After all, we are the people who conquered the West, traveled to Antarctica, and landed on the moon.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What is your favorite military equipment to operate?
Answer: This is kind of surprising, but in my experience, I had a ton of fun with the M203 grenade launcher. I was deadly accurate with it and I could easily put a grenade through the window of a house or skip it under a vehicle. The recoil is also not too bad. It’s an incredibly fun weapon system once you get used to it. (A soldier operating an M4 with an attached M203 grenade launcher. This weapon system is incredibly easy to operate and very cool to use. Photo credit: US Army.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Do most of the people you know own guns?
Answer: Most of the people I know in the United States own guns, yes. I’m from Michigan and I have lived in Arizona, Ohio, and Minnesota. All places with a deeply ingrained gun/hunting culture. Additionally, I’m a military police veteran and previously worked for a police department. If you wanted to put together a resume for a person likely to own guns in America and to know many gun-owning people — it would be someone like me. To people from other parts of the world and even to some people who live in my very liberal Ohio suburb, this is shocking. They believe that all gun owners sit around and masturbate to the newest edition of Guns and Ammo. (Quesadillas with pumpkin salsa. A regional speciality from Yucatán that I learned to cook during my time there. Photo by author.) Maybe this applies to other people, but owning guns is not a part of my identity or anything like that. I have a couple of university degrees, careers in several disparate industries. I also love to run, hike, cook, paint, travel, and write. Most of those things interest me more than shooting. Why is it that once I tell someone I own guns that it often becomes the defining aspect of my personality? Weird. I think they’re more obsessed with guns than I am.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: How much does a US citizen travel in a year and mostly where?
Answer: It depends on who you ask. I’m a US citizen. This year I have spent two months in Brazil, three months in Colombia, a month in Mexico, two weeks in Florida, a weekend in Texas, a week in Michigan. There’s still a few months left in the year yet. What’s nice this time of year? (Watching the sunrise the morning of my 39th birthday. This year is the first year I have really gotten back to traveling like I wanted to since the plague-that-shall-not-be-named. It’s been one of the most interesting for sure. Photo by author.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: For dating, how important is it that a guy needs to be over six feet and makes six figures?
Answer: I’m a 5’8 guy. Based on personal experiences and observations, the height thing is a factor with very few women. Most women are open to dating a guy who is shorter than six foot, since most of the men in the world are not six foot tall. This is just a reality. I often see this six foot quote and I really think it comes from some incel-type dudes that want to tell themselves the reason no one wants to date them is because of their stature. The fact that they lack gainful employment, have a neck beard, own a collection of manga, and sit around watching internet porn all day is conveniently left out. You don’t need to make six figures, but you should be able to make enough money to take care of yourself before you get out there into the dating market as an adult. Some women won’t date you because you don’t make enough money. Some women won’t date you because you’re not tall enough. Others will reject you for other reasons. This is all very normal and although rejection stings, you just keep going. In time, the ones who rejected you will surely be outnumbered by the ones who didn’t. However, it takes a winner’s mentality to see things that way. You won’t find that in the kind of man who makes excuses because of his height or income. (The author, a “short king.”)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Why does everyone love rare/medium rare meat so much?
Answer: Of course this can never be anything but an opinion subject to endless to debate, but it’s the best way to eat your steak. Anything else is simply a waste of good meat. Imagine buying a good cut of ribeye and cooking it until it’s dry in the middle. I call that a waste of money. (A steak I prepared just the way I like it. Potatoes are optional. Photo by author.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What is something that you're one of the few people to ever see?
Answer: A terrorist attack might be one of those things. One morning in Baghdad I was just leaving my post and heading back to my quarters to get some sleep. Suddenly, I heard the sound of an enormous blast followed by a mushroom cloud I could clearly see on the horizon. Unforgettable. Apparently there was a vehicle borne explosive set off in downtown Baghdad. The vehicle was packed with hundreds of pounds of explosives and something like 200 people were killed (I learned this later from CNN). Sure, I didn’t see it up close, but it’s one of those things that’s forever stuck in my memory knowing that I was witness to a moment where hundreds of people were wiped out in an instant. (The area formerly known as the Victory Base Complex (VBC), Baghdad, Iraq. Photo by author.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: How do you make sure you can live an action-packed life at all times?
Answer: You don’t and even if you could, you wouldn’t want to. Take for example, the movie Top Gun, with Tom Cruise who plays the role of our hero pilot, Pete Mitchell. In the span of a 110 minute movie we get to see our hero tango with evil commies over the Indian Ocean in a fighter jet, ride motorcycles, play volleyball with the bros on a picturesque beach, make love to a beautiful woman, get into an aircraft accident where he loses his friend, and finally (in a very unlikely scenario) called from training to take a mission of utmost importance to go fight the evil commies again. He gets into a dogfight where he successfully blows up several enemy aircraft with missiles. All within a 110 minute movie. (Pete Mitchell can only exist in a fantasy world. There is no real life equivalent of him and there never will be. Image source: Reddit.) Supposing the events depicted in Top Gun were actually possible for one pilot to experience in a short amount of time. There’s tons the movie doesn’t show you! The movie doesn’t show you that Pete Mitchell has to attend four boring years of college to be eligible to be a pilot. During that time he is in Navy ROTC, where he must do boring things like shine shoes and boots, perfectly iron his uniform, and take many exams and memorize mundane facts about Naval history. He then has to attend undergraduate pilot training after graduating college, where he will then spend an enormous amount of classroom time learning about the technical aspects of flying an aircraft, navigation, and radio communication, all before he ever handles the controls of an aircraft. After a couple of years of training and being certified as a pilot, Mitchell will then be sent to the fleet where much of his time will be attending briefings and waiting around for something, anything to happen. When actually flying, probably 90% or more of his flights will be completely uneventful. After Mitchell actually does get to experience action a few times, he ends up extremely traumatized due to the death of his friend and RIO, Goose. He has screaming fits of PTSD which sometimes wake him up at night. And oh, he still has an unresolved case of the clap he picked up on a port call in Hong Kong one time. He carelessly gives it to his instructor-girlfriend, Charlie, who later unceremoniously dumps him. He’s also been ticketed by the MA’s for not wearing a helmet while riding a motorcycle on a Navy installation. Eventually he has his motorcycle impounded after repeated offenses. You get the point. Life is not a movie or an adventure novel. No matter how bold or daring you might be in life, much of your life will be spent doing mundane and uninteresting things, just for the 10% or (likely) less of the time you actually get to do things that excite you. Then some of the things that excite you have a not-so-insignificant chance of terrifying you. By all means, lead an adventurous life, I approve of it. However, there is no way to lead a life that is action-packed at all times in reality. That’s just a fantasy best left to Hollywood.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Would bodybuilders make good soldiers in the army?
Answer: Like many things in life, the answer depends. But particularly since your question included the word “good” and not the best soldiers, I can say that in some cases, yes, bodybuilders can make good soldiers. This is even more possible on the modern battlefield in militaries like the United States where modern fighting is often times more akin to what would have been mechanized infantry in WWII. In other words, you’re more likely to spend a good deal of your time doing mounted patrols. Every military unit has at least few guys (and even gals) that are into bodybuilding. There were a couple of bodybuilders in my unit. One was a man in his early 30’s at the time, and one of our first sergeants, a woman, who was nearly 40 years old. Both were about 6ft tall and well over 200lbs. The thing is, you actually can be rather big and still have good endurance, if you train for it. Of course, we’re also not talking about professional bodybuilders, but amateurs, who, although they will be larger than average, won’t be beating Ronnie Coleman at Mr. Olympia. Now, a lot of people here on Quora will tell you that special operations personnel tend to be thin and wiry. This may be true during their initial ascension training, but, in-country, many SOF soldiers would come to our gym, since naturally, the Air Force had the best gym. At least a few of them were definitely on the bigger side of normal and enjoyed weight lifting. That a few were on PED’s, was obvious, in my opinion. These were the guys mostly going out on snatch and grab missions at night in Baghdad while mounted on humvees or other vehicles. Hardly a job that required the endurance of a marathon runner. (Arnold in his prime. He would likely at least make a good soldier in today’s US Army. Photo credit: Wikipedia.) Edit: just as a case in point, Taylor Cavanaugh, a rather infamous Navy SEAL, was kicked out of the teams specifically because of his PED use. Later on he became a member of the French Foreign Legion. (Taylor Cavanaugh, former SEAL and Legionnaire. Photo credit: Taylorcavanaugh.com.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What is the hottest club you have been to?
Answer: Clubbing in Mexico City is insane and really cool. I went to some club in Roma Norte on the recommendation of others with five or six (mostly)Australians that were hanging with me. The clubs there stay open until 4 or 5 a.m. and sometimes beyond. Absolutely packed to the gills. The best part to me though: you can find an excellent taco stand outside when you’re extremely drunk and hungry. Mexico City clubs: 10/10. I highly recommend! (Out clubbing in Roma Norte, Mexico City. I don’t really go to clubs anymore these days, but there was a time. Photo by author.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Would you rather receive one million US dollars or flip a coin for the chance to win one billion US dollars?
Answer: Yeah, so…a million dollars isn’t enough money to substantially change my life as it exists today. So, I’m going to go for broke, baby! If I don’t get the billion dollars I think I would be quite satisfied knowing that at least I tried. If I do get it, I’ll buy Lichtenstein or some other small country. “Yesterday we were an army with no country. Tomorrow, we have to decide which country we want to buy!”

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Why should I not complain in life?
Answer: Mind you, this isn’t true 100% of the time, but usually we shouldn’t complain because almost everyone that you might complain to has something they could complain about too. These last few years it’s incredibly rare to know someone who hasn’t suffered some kind of personal tragedy or endured some period of hardship. People with a sick parent or spouse, the loss of a close loved one, the ending of a marriage, or long term relationship. Personal financial or health difficulties. When we complain it’s often times because we have failed to take stock of all the things in our life that have gone right. Express gratitude for the things you have right now, even the small things. Especially if you woke up with a roof over your head, food to eat, and in relatively good health (which is actually no minor thing).

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: How do American cops differ from British ones? Is one system considered better or worse than the other?
Answer: American cops are VERY hesitant to interact with people on the street. Just approaching a cop on the streets in the US in 2024 feels a little risky, because they don’t know who you are, if you’re armed, and if you have bad intentions. A couple of years ago I remember that I was going to a football game (American football, of course), and as I approached the stadium there were several SWAT officers and a tactical vehicle parked in front. I remember that I went for my wallet to retrieve my ticket and one of the officers placed his hand on his gun as a precautionary measure. I was just an ordinary football fan, but I was aware of the fact that if I had likely moved too rapidly or alarmingly, the officer would have blown me away. In the UK I knew that, on the Tube, for example, if I got lost, it would be totally fine to approach an officer from the British Transport Police or The Met and let them know that I was lost and needed help getting back to my hotel. This is exactly what happened one night. The officers were extremely courteous and gracious. I don’t think this is something that is even possible in the US, the police in the US have a different attitude because it’s a different level of danger and a more dangerous culture. I think the British method of policing is a model for the entire world to follow though. Just my opinion. (Officers of the British Transport Police. If you get lost in London, let them know, and they’ll help you out. Photo credit: Daily Mail.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Do Americans really avoid hospitals, even in serious situations because of the bills that follow after?
Answer: For me, this has never been an issue. When I was young and we had very little household income, we qualified for the state Medicaid program which usually covered most or all of the cost of going to a hospital. As an adult, I have been able to go to the Veterans Affairs hospital or to the nearest hospital to me in a serious emergency and they would cover the bill. Contrary to what a lot of people may say, my care at our veteran’s hospitals has almost always been at least good or excellent. I had some problems when I lived in an area with a lot of veterans (Phoenix), where I would get longer wait times for an appointment for routine medical care. However, in an emergency, it was never an issue to show up to the ER. In Cleveland, this isn’t an issue at all. In fact, I will often times travel back to the United States just for my medical appointments. At times, I get a same day appointment if I call and have an urgent, but not serious problem. I have absolute trust in my care team. I still have private insurance, but I haven’t used it in many years because I prefer to go to the Veterans Affairs hospital that has my entire medical history dating back to the age of 20. (Louis Stokes Veterans Affairs hospital. Not only have I liked my care here, but I really like my doctor who really pushed me to get into better shape and to take care of my health. Photo credit: VA.gov)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What aspect of everyday modern life is underrated?
Answer: I can think of so many, but here are just a few of the best: Travel: going just 10 miles used to be quite a journey just over a hundred years ago. Today, such a journey is routine. Even the worst modern cars are more comfortable, quieter, safer than the very first generation of cars. Since we have cars, we don’t have to find places in our cities to dispose of horse shit. Leading to my next point… Smell: most of us rarely deal with unpleasant smells on a day-to-day basis in the modern world. This was not the case for many of our ancestors. (Indigenous people using a smartphone. Photo credit: National Geographic). Communication: with nearly anyone, anywhere in the world. Instantly. Just 30 years ago calling people outside of your region or state was a pain. Almost no one used email yet. Today, cell phones make us anxious if we see someone has gone ten minutes without reading our message. Safe food and water: although not everyone in the world has guaranteed access to these things, the percentage that do is higher than ever. We shouldn’t take this for granted. Choice: we have the ability to choose from an ever-increasing variety of foods, flavors, hobbies, careers, destinations, and romantic partners (thanks to the reach of dating apps). We don’t talk enough about how unusual this is in human history. Travel 2: the distances we can travel in less than a day. A few days ago I was in a completely different climate zone, with people speaking a different language, eating different food while listening to different music. Most of the people also had a different appearance. Later that day I was thousands of miles away on a different continent with different weather, language, food, music, and people. Sometimes the rapid change in scenery and climate actually messes with you a little bit. For most of human history this journey would have been impossible. 400 years ago it would have been a dangerous proposition that would have taken months. (Richard Westall’s Sword of Damocles. Wikipedia). What do we pay for all these glorious benefits? Humanity has the power to destroy life as we know it in a single afternoon. Compared to our ancestors we live like kings and queens. But above the throne on which we sit hangs the sword of Damocles.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Do you live a simple lifestyle?
Answer: This depends on who you ask. On one hand I get to spend a large amount of my life traveling, which is a privilege to be sure. On the other hand, I own few physical possessions, particularly in comparison to others my age from my country. I own only a small apartment, no car, no TV. For the majority of the year I am happy living out of two bags that carry both cold weather and warm weather clothing. I’m usually ready to travel just about anywhere at a moment’s notice from anywhere else in the world. Having few physical possessions is incredibly liberating. Here’s the catch: living a minimalist lifestyle is, more often than not, something that very few people can actually afford. It takes money to have less. Most people, for example, couldn’t live in the US without a car. I am easily able to do so for the few months I spend there every year.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Why were 100 flights cancelled at Frankfurt airport because climate protesters glued themselves to the runaway, when these protesters weren't big enough to stop planes weighing many tons?
Answer: Actually, things much smaller than people can completely fuck up an aircraft engine. It’s why at every airfield I’ve ever worked on they are obsessive about checking for foreign object debris or FOD. Things protesters carry like car or home keys, articles of clothing, and electronic devices can easily become FOD that is ingested by a jet engine. This can result in millions of dollars in damage and pose a risk to the lives of everyone onboard an aircraft. I have worked at both military and civilian airports. Posters like the ones below are common in buildings exiting onto a flight ramp. Guarding against FOD is the business of everyone who works at an airfield. (Source: Reddit) (Source: DOD) (Source: DOD) FOD walks are frequently conducted to check for anything on the airfield that might be ingested by an aircraft engine: (Airmen conducting a FOD walk to ensure the airfield is perfectly clear of debris. Note: even hats are prohibited for flight line personnel, so that they do not become a source of FOD. Source: US Air Force).

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Do you split the bill when you go on a date? Why?
Answer: Sometimes. This mostly happens when I am in the US or Europe, where often times women will volunteer to split half the bill with me. If they do, I typically don’t refuse, because arguing just makes things awkward. In Latin America this is never a concern: men are expected to pay for dates the great majority of the time. However, the important thing is that no matter where I am going on a date, I am always prepared to pay for the entire date/meal. (Studying the menu carefully at Restaurante Les Présidents in São Paulo, Brazil. If for some reason your credit card is declined here, they employ giant bouncers that will crush your bones! Photo by author.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What is the likelihood of someone obtaining a federal job?
Answer: US Government: I can’t speak for today, but in 2012 when I started, the odds were slim. None of my classmates could figure out what to do to land a phone call, let alone an interview. I probably uploaded my resume to the federal government website and applied to thousands of jobs before even netting just a few calls back. Then there was an interview, and an on-boarding process (to include background checks, reference checks, and a probationary period). Even having veteran’s preference and finishing my master’s degree didn’t get me very far ahead of the field. Some of it was just luck and sheer number of resumes sent out. This was all to land a GS-7 position, but my career ladder lead me to GS-12 fairly quickly. I was only unhappy with my salary for a year or so, then I got overtime which meant an almost insane amount of money for a government employee at times (plus bonuses). There is also huge potential for investment profits if you invest your TSP intelligently with generous government matching. Of course, the job outlook is a general statement. Some specialities will have no problems obtaining a government job like doctors, nurses, and some engineers. These fields are pretty much always in demand.
